about: Nine Tails RULES 쇼츠 편성표(2026-10-05 사용자: '어린 친구·청년 타깃, 도파민·자극성·중독성' → 동아시아 규칙괴담 매일 쇼츠). 루틴은 `python gumiho/tales/rules.py next --date <오늘>` 이 준 한 편만 쓴다(날짜로 결정론적 배정 — start 부터 하루 한 편, 목록 순서대로). format: rules(규칙 4–5개 + 어긋나는 마지막 규칙 → 처음으로 루프) · versus(괴물 대결, 설화 근거로 판정 + 댓글 투표) · pov(2인칭 '너' 생존). facts 는 확인된 뼈대(규칙은 반드시 여기서 — 지어내지 않는다), careful 은 단정하면 안 되는 것. 목록이 바닥나기 전에 주간 검토가 PR 로 채운다.

rules.title_idea: If Someone Calls Your Name Three Times at Night, Don't Answer
rules.premise: In Korea and China, many grandparents still warn: a voice calling your name in the dark may not be a person.
facts: A widespread East Asian folk belief: spirits (or reapers) call a living person's name at night; answering lets them take your soul — so you don't answer until you are sure who it is
Korean jeoseung saja (reapers) are said to come for the dying by name, often in threes, carrying a register of names
At traditional Korean funerals families set out saja-bap (three bowls of rice, straw sandals, coins) for the reapers
A common version: a voice calls only once or twice; a real person will call again, a spirit will not wait — wait for the third call
careful: Versions differ by region (some say twice, some three times) — present it as 'they say', not one fixed rule
No real deaths or real people

rules.title_idea: Never Whistle at Night in Korea or Japan
rules.premise: Whistling after dark is one of the most common taboos in both Korea and Japan — and the reasons get worse the more you ask.
facts: Korea: whistling at night is said to call snakes, ghosts or bad spirits into the house
Japan: whistling at night (yobue) is said to summon snakes, ghosts, or in some regions bandits/kidnappers (tengu in some tellings)
Parents in both countries still use the taboo to keep children quiet at night
careful: Regional variation — say 'in some regions'
Don't claim anyone was harmed

rules.title_idea: If a Masked Woman Asks 'Am I Pretty?' — Never Say Yes or No
rules.premise: A woman in a surgical mask stops you on the way home and asks one question. Every honest answer is wrong.
facts: Kuchisake-onna (slit-mouthed woman) is a Japanese urban legend; a panic spread among schoolchildren in 1979 and some schools had children walk home in groups
She asks 'Am I pretty?' (watashi kirei?); answering no or yes both lead to danger in the legend
Survival tricks in versions of the legend: answer 'you're average' / 'so-so', ask her the same question back, throw hard candy (bekko ame) she stops to pick up, or say the word 'pomade' three times
A Korean version of the legend circulated as the 'red mask' (빨간 마스크) story
careful: No gore — never show the wound; imply it
Don't depict a real person

rules.title_idea: Never Look at the Woman Who Gets On at Floor 5 — The Elevator Game
rules.premise: An internet ritual: ride an elevator alone through a sequence of floors to reach 'another world'. The rules are exact.
facts: The Elevator Game is an internet ritual: alone in a building with at least 10 floors, press 4, 2, 6, 2, 10, then 5
At the 5th floor a young woman may get on — do not look at her and do not speak to her
Then press 1; if the elevator goes up to the 10th floor instead, you are said to arrive in 'the other world' where you are the only person
To leave, players say you must ride back down by the same sequence; if anything feels wrong, don't get out
careful: It is an internet legend (claimed Korean origin is disputed) — say 'the internet says'
Do not encourage trespassing; elevator scene only

rules.title_idea: Never Leave One-Man Hide and Seek Unfinished
rules.premise: A Japanese ritual where you play hide-and-seek with a doll — alone, at 3 a.m. Its rules on how to END it matter most.
facts: Hitori kakurenbo (one-person hide-and-seek) is a Japanese internet ritual
Players stuff a doll with rice and their own nail clippings, sew it with red thread, give it a name, and put it in a bathtub of water at 3 a.m.
The player says 'you're it' to the doll, hides with a cup of salt water, and must stay silent with the lights and TV off/static
To end it, the player must find the doll, spit/pour salt water on it and say 'I win' three times — players are warned never to leave the ritual unfinished
careful: Never show self-harm; no instructions with blood
Present as a legend, not a real procedure to try — end with 'don't try this'

rules.title_idea: Dokkaebi vs Kappa: Who Wins a Wrestling Match?
rules.premise: Korea's goblin and Japan's river imp both LOVE wrestling humans. Put them in a ring.
facts: Dokkaebi (Korean goblins) love ssireum wrestling and challenge travelers on night roads; folk tales say you can beat one by tripping its left leg
Dokkaebi love buckwheat jelly and fear horse blood in some tales; they carry a magic club (dokkaebi bangmangi)
Kappa (Japanese river imps) also challenge people to sumo wrestling; they have a water-filled dish on their head
If you bow to a kappa, it politely bows back and spills the water from its dish, losing its strength
careful: Regional versions differ (left/right leg) — say 'in many tales'
Keep it fun, no violence beyond wrestling
End with a comments vote

rules.title_idea: POV: You See Something White Wiggling in the Rice Field
rules.premise: You're visiting the countryside in summer. Far across the rice field, something white is wiggling. Don't look closer.
facts: Kunekune is a Japanese internet legend (2000s): a white, thin figure seen wiggling far away in rice fields on hot summer days
Seeing it from far away is said to be fine; understanding what it is — especially through binoculars — is said to drive you mad
In the best-known telling, two brothers see it; the one who looks through binoculars is changed
careful: Internet legend — say so
No mental-illness mockery; keep it eerie, not clinical

rules.title_idea: Never Pick Up Money on the Street During Ghost Month
rules.premise: For one lunar month a year, Chinese tradition says the gates of the underworld open and the hungry ghosts walk among us.
facts: Ghost Month is the seventh lunar month in Chinese tradition; the Hungry Ghost Festival (Zhongyuan) falls on the 15th night
Common taboos: don't swim (water ghosts may pull you under), don't go out late at night, don't whistle
Don't pick up money or red envelopes you find on the street; don't step on or kick roadside offerings
Don't hang clothes outside overnight; leave the front row of seats empty at ghost-month street operas — they are for the ghosts
careful: Practices vary across China, Taiwan, Malaysia, Singapore — say 'in many places'
Respectful — it's a living tradition

rules.title_idea: Never Write Someone's Name in Red Ink in Korea
rules.premise: Ask any Korean student and they'll stop you mid-sentence: not in red.
facts: In Korea, writing a living person's name in red ink is a strong taboo — it is said to wish death or bad luck on them
One common explanation: names of the deceased were traditionally written in red on registers or banners
Many Koreans still avoid red pens for names on cards, letters and exam papers
careful: Origins are debated — give 'one explanation'
Light, not mocking

rules.title_idea: Never Play Bunshinsaba Alone — Korean Students Know Why
rules.premise: Two students hold one pen over paper and chant words they don't understand. The pen starts to move.
facts: Bunshinsaba (분신사바) is a spirit-summoning game played by Korean students, similar to Ouija or Japan's Kokkuri-san
Two people hold one pen together over paper and chant 'bunshinsaba, bunshinsaba, please come'
Rules passed between students: never let go of the pen, never play alone, and always ask the spirit to leave before stopping
A 2004 Korean horror film named Bunshinsaba made the game famous
careful: Don't depict the film's scenes
Present as a school legend; end with 'don't try this'

rules.title_idea: If a Hopping Corpse Is Near, Hold Your Breath
rules.premise: In old China, corpses walked home at night in single file — and they could find you by your breath.
facts: Jiangshi (僵尸) are reanimated 'stiff corpses' of Chinese folklore that hop with arms outstretched
They are said to find the living by sensing breath — holding your breath can hide you
Folk remedies: sticky rice, mirrors (they fear their reflection), peach-wood swords, and a Taoist priest's paper talisman on the forehead
Linked to the 'corpse walkers' of Xiangxi, Hunan, said to guide the dead home at night
careful: No gore
Hopping imagery can be eerie-fun

rules.title_idea: Jangsanbeom vs the Slit-Mouthed Woman: Who Would Win?
rules.premise: Korea's voice-stealing mountain beast vs Japan's masked woman. Both trick you with words.
facts: Jangsanbeom is a Korean urban legend (popular from the 2010s) of a white-furred creature on Mount Jang said to mimic human voices, like a family member calling you
Kuchisake-onna (Japan) asks 'Am I pretty?' and can be escaped with tricks such as answering 'you're average' or throwing hard candy
Both legends turn on speech: one copies voices, the other punishes answers
careful: Comic-biased verdict from Gumi, grounded in the legends' rules
End with a vote

rules.title_idea: Never Knock on the Third Stall: The Rules of Hanako-san
rules.premise: Every Japanese school kid knows which bathroom stall you leave alone.
facts: Hanako-san of the toilet is a Japanese school legend: a girl's spirit in the third stall of a girls' bathroom, often on the third floor
The ritual: knock three times on the third stall and ask 'Hanako-san, are you there?'
In many versions a voice answers 'Yes, I'm here' — and what happens next depends on the school
careful: No gore; no bathroom imagery beyond doors/corridors
School legend — say so

rules.title_idea: POV: You Swim Alone at Dusk and Something Holds Your Ankle
rules.premise: Second person: you swim out alone as the sun goes down. Korean grandmothers had a rule for this.
facts: Mul gwishin (물귀신) are Korean water ghosts of people who drowned, said to pull swimmers under to take their place
Korean saying 'to drag someone down like a water ghost' (물귀신 작전) comes from this belief
Traditional advice: don't swim alone, don't swim at dusk or at night
careful: Water-safety tone at the end is fine
No drowning depiction — cut before

rules.title_idea: Never Give Anyone Four of Anything in Korea
rules.premise: Step into a Korean elevator. Floor 3, then F. Where did 4 go?
facts: In Korean, Chinese and Japanese, the word for four sounds like the word for death (사/sì/shi)
Many buildings in Korea label the 4th floor 'F'; some hospitals and hotels skip it entirely
Gifts in sets of four are avoided in many East Asian families
careful: Tetraphobia is cultural, not supernatural — mix fact with eerie tone, don't claim harm

rules.title_idea: If a Kappa Challenges You, Bow First
rules.premise: A child-sized creature climbs out of the river and asks you to wrestle. Your manners will save you.
facts: Kappa are Japanese river creatures (yokai) with a water-filled dish on their head and a beak
Bowing to a kappa makes it bow back politely and spill the water from its dish, which weakens it
Kappa are said to love cucumbers; families once wrote names on cucumbers and threw them in rivers to protect children
Signs near Japanese rivers sometimes still show kappa as a warning to children
careful: Older legends include grim details — skip them

rules.title_idea: Never Stand in the Middle of a Three-Person Photo
rules.premise: Three friends line up for a photo. Nobody wants the middle. There's a reason.
facts: A Japanese superstition (also known in Korea) says the person in the middle of a photo of three will die first or have bad luck
It dates back to early photography in Japan (Meiji era) when photos were rare
People sometimes hold a stuffed toy or doll to make the group 'four'
careful: Contradiction: four is unlucky too — that's the twist, play it for the loop

rules.title_idea: Never Stick Your Chopsticks Upright in Rice
rules.premise: It looks harmless. Every grandmother at the table will gasp.
facts: In Korea, Japan and China, chopsticks stuck upright in a bowl of rice resemble incense sticks or offerings for the dead
In Japan, it echoes the bowl of rice placed for the deceased at funerals (makura-meshi)
Passing food from chopsticks to chopsticks is also taboo in Japan because it mirrors moving cremated bones at funerals
careful: Cultural etiquette — eerie, respectful

rules.title_idea: Korea's Grim Reaper vs Japan's Shinigami: Which One Comes for You?
rules.premise: Two countries, two ways to be collected. Gumi judges.
facts: Korean jeoseung saja escort the dead to the afterlife, often in black robes and a black gat hat, carrying a register of names
Families offer saja-bap (rice, straw sandals, coins) to the reapers at traditional funerals
Shinigami ('death gods') in Japanese culture are mostly a modern idea shaped by Edo-period stories and later manga/anime
careful: Don't depict Death Note or KPop Demon Hunters characters
Vote at the end

rules.title_idea: Never Count the School Stairs After Dark
rules.premise: Twelve steps in the daytime. Count them at night.
facts: A common school ghost story in Korea and Japan: the staircase has one extra step at night (12 becomes 13)
In Korean school legends (학교 괴담) statues such as Admiral Yi or King Sejong are said to move at midnight
Japan's 'seven wonders of the school' (gakkō no nana fushigi) include counting stairs
careful: School legend — say so

rules.title_idea: If the Snow Woman Spares You, Never Tell Anyone
rules.premise: In a blizzard a woman made of snow lets you live — on one condition.
facts: In Lafcadio Hearn's 'Yuki-Onna' (Kwaidan, 1904) the snow woman kills the old woodcutter Mosaku with her breath and spares young Minokichi
Her condition: never tell anyone about that night
Years later Minokichi tells his wife the story — and she reveals she is the snow woman
careful: Keep the twist for the loop: the person you tell might be her

rules.title_idea: If You Remember This Word at 20, You Die — The Purple Mirror
rules.premise: A Japanese internet legend that works like a curse: once you hear the word, you're in.
facts: Murasaki kagami (purple mirror) is a Japanese urban legend: if you still remember the words 'purple mirror' on your 20th birthday, you will die
Versions add a counter-word that cancels it (often 'white water lily' / shiroi suishō in tellings)
It spread among Japanese schoolchildren in the 1990s
careful: It's a chain-curse meme — make it playful-creepy, not threatening to the viewer; end by giving the 'cancel' word

rules.title_idea: POV: A Pop-Up Asks 'Do You Like the Red Room?'
rules.premise: You close the pop-up. It opens again. The voice asks again.
facts: The Red Room curse is a Japanese internet legend (late 1990s Flash animation): a pop-up asks 'Do you like the red room?'
If you can't close it, you are said to be found in a room painted red
It is one of the earliest internet horror legends
careful: No blood imagery — red light and walls only
Internet legend — say so

rules.title_idea: Never Sleep With a Fan On in Korea (Or So They Say)
rules.premise: Korea's most famous modern superstition — and why fans there have timers.
facts: Fan death (선풍기 사망) is the belief that sleeping in a closed room with an electric fan running can kill you
Many electric fans sold in Korea have a sleep timer that shuts them off
Doctors and scientists dispute it; the belief faded among young Koreans but is still widely known
careful: Must say it's a myth/disputed — eerie framing, factual ending

rules.title_idea: If a Stranger Offers to Walk You Over the Mountain, Count Her Tails
rules.premise: Gumi's own rules — the legend of the nine-tailed fox, told by the fox.
facts: The gumiho is a Korean nine-tailed fox who can take the form of a beautiful woman
In the fox-bead (yeowoo guseul) tale she passes a bead to a young man through kisses to steal his energy over 100 days
Legends say a gumiho who doesn't eat human flesh/livers for 1,000 days (or keeps her secret 100 days) can become human
careful: No gore (liver) — imply
Gumi can wink at the camera here

rules.title_idea: Never Buy Your Boyfriend Shoes in Korea
rules.premise: A sweet gift that every Korean auntie will warn you about.
facts: In Korea, giving shoes to a romantic partner is said to make them 'walk away' from you
A common workaround: the receiver pays a small coin for the shoes so it becomes a purchase, not a gift
careful: Light rule — use as a breather in the week; twist can be funny

rules.title_idea: If a Goblin Challenges You to Wrestle at Night, Aim for His Left Leg
rules.premise: Korea's goblins don't eat you. They just won't let you go home until dawn.
facts: Dokkaebi are Korean goblin spirits often born from old household objects (a broom, a pestle) touched by human blood
They challenge travelers to ssireum wrestling through the night; many tales say trip the left leg to win
In the morning, the 'goblin' you fought is often found to be an old broom tied to a tree
careful: Left/right varies by tale — 'in many tales'

rules.title_idea: If Your Mother Calls You From the Trees on Mount Jang, Don't Turn Around
rules.premise: The voice is perfect. Your mother is at home.
facts: Jangsanbeom is a Korean urban legend (popular from the 2010s) of a white-furred creature on Mount Jang in Busan
It is said to mimic the voices of family members to lure people deeper into the mountain
Hikers' advice in the legend: don't answer a familiar voice in the woods; leave the mountain before dark
careful: Mount Jang is a real hiking area — no trespassing or panic about a real place; say 'the legend says'
